FACT_ID: sec03-R01 | anchor: A31
A driver must submit to a drug-concentration chemical test when probable cause indicates operation under the influence of a drug other than alcohol. [A31]
Source: [A31 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-R02 | anchor: A32
An administrative OUI-related suspension continues even if the driver is later found not guilty of OUI. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R03 | anchor: A32
If police testimony leads to an OUI conviction, a test refusal is an aggravating factor and an additional OUI suspension is added. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R04 | anchor: A32
For a first OUI court conviction at 0.08–0.14 grams of alcohol in a 100-milliliter blood sample or 210-liter breath sample, the minimum fine is $500, rising to $600 for refusal. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R05 | anchor: A32
After a first OUI conviction in the 0.08–0.14 category, measured as grams of alcohol in 100 milliliters of blood or in 210 liters of breath, the driver loses the license for at least 150 days, pays a reinstatement fee and completes alcohol-and-drug education and treatment. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R06 | anchor: A32
First-conviction OUI aggravators include 0.15 grams of alcohol or more in 100 milliliters of blood or in 210 liters of breath, exceeding the speed limit by at least 30 miles per hour, eluding police, test refusal or carrying a passenger younger than 21. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R07 | anchor: A32
The first-conviction aggravated OUI category requires at least 48 hours in jail, increased to 96 hours for test refusal. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R08 | anchor: A32
The aggravated first-OUI-conviction category also requires at least 150 days of license loss, a reinstatement fee and alcohol-and-drug education and treatment. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R09 | anchor: A32
A second or later OUI offender must show liability-insurance proof before license reinstatement. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R10 | anchor: A32
No work or limited license is available during the minimum OUI-conviction suspension period. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R11 | anchor: A32
A license reinstated after an OUI conviction is conditional on driving with no alcohol in the person’s system. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R12 | anchor: A33
The reinstated license remains conditional for 1 year after a first OUI conviction and 10 years after a second or later conviction. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R13 | anchor: A33
A conditional licensee driving with any alcohol faces a 1-year suspension without a preliminary hearing. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R14 | anchor: A33
A conditional licensee operating at 0.08 grams or more per 100 milliliters of blood or 210 liters of breath faces the suspension periods applicable to second or third OUI convictions. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R15 | anchor: A33
A conditional licensee’s alcohol-test refusal brings a 2-year suspension added to any earlier OUI-conviction suspension. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R16 | anchor: A33
Prescription and nonprescription drugs can impair driving, and having obtained a drug legally is not a defense to impaired operation. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R17 | anchor: A33
Some nonprescription cold, allergy, headache or calming remedies cause drowsiness, while stimulant or diet pills can cause nervousness, dizziness or poor focus. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R18 | anchor: A33
Read drug labels and ask a doctor or pharmacist about driving safety when the effects are uncertain. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R19 | anchor: A33
Amphetamine stimulants can reduce concentration or cause hallucinations, with tiredness and depression possible as effects wear off. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R20 | anchor: A33
Combining tranquilizers with alcohol can cause dizziness or drowsiness. [A33]
Source: [A33 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R21 | anchor: A34
Excessive barbiturate use can cause drowsiness, confusion, poor coordination, tremors and difficulty thinking clearly. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R22 | anchor: A34
Marijuana can cause drowsiness and impaired judgment of time and space. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R23 | anchor: A34
Some marijuana users focus on a single object and neglect other surroundings. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R24 | anchor: A34
Illegal drugs can impair reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R25 | anchor: A34
Alcohol combined with another drug can amplify impairment and add dangerous effects beyond those of either substance alone. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R26 | anchor: A34
Do not combine drinking with other drugs or drive after alcohol or impairing-drug use. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R27 | anchor: A34
A conviction for drug-impaired driving carries the punishments applied to alcohol-impaired driving, whether the drug was legal or illegal. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R28 | anchor: A34
An OUI arrest, or an arrest for driving after an OUI-related suspension, can bring vehicle seizure, towing and storage costs, and exposure to a fine and jail. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R29 | anchor: A34
A driver involved in a fatal crash or one likely to cause death must submit to a chemical test; refusal brings a 1-year license suspension. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R30 | anchor: A34
When the Secretary of State finds that alcohol- or drug-impaired negligent driving caused a death, the license is immediately suspended for at least 1 year in addition to any chemical-test-refusal suspension. [A34]
Source: [A34 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R31 | anchor: A35
A vehicular-homicide conviction brings an extended prison term and at least 5 years of license revocation; intoxication at the offense makes the revocation permanent. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R32 | anchor: A35
On a public road, the operator violates the open-container law when the operator or a passenger consumes alcohol or has an open alcoholic container in the passenger area, subject to the listed exceptions. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R33 | anchor: A35
In a vehicle without a trunk, an open alcoholic container is excepted when kept behind the last upright seat or in an area not normally occupied by an operator or passenger. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R34 | anchor: A35
The open-container exception for a fare-paying passenger applies in a vehicle designed for hired passenger transportation other than a taxicab. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R35 | anchor: A35
A passenger may possess an open alcoholic container or consume alcohol in the living quarters of a motor home, trailer, semitrailer or truck camper under the listed exception. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R36 | anchor: A35
Alcohol transport to or from a catered event is excepted when the operator or employer holds a valid off-premise catering license. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R37 | anchor: A35
An OUI conviction creates a criminal record. [A35]
Source: [A35 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R38 | anchor: A36
Alcohol is a depressant even if an initial small amount makes someone feel livelier. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R39 | anchor: A36
A person younger than 21 may not buy alcohol. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R40 | anchor: A36
A person younger than 21 may transport alcohol in a vehicle only within employment duties or at a parent’s or guardian’s request. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R41 | anchor: A36
Transporting illegal drugs in a motor vehicle is prohibited. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R42 | anchor: A36
For a driver younger than 21, any blood alcohol while operating or refusal of blood or breath testing brings at least 1 year of license loss. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R43 | anchor: A36
For Maine OUI rules, licenses issued to people younger than 21 are considered provisional and subject to immediate suspension until age 21. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R44 | anchor: A36
Do not ride with someone who has been drinking; use a taxi, bus or a sober friend or relative instead. [A36]
Source: [A36 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-R45 | anchor: A37
Strong worry, excitement, fear, anger or sadness can impair thinking and response to road hazards. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R46 | anchor: A37
If emotions interfere with driving, wait until more composed, allow extra travel time or ask another person to drive. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R47 | anchor: A37
Even temporary illness or a minor physical problem can affect driving, so let another person drive when you are unwell. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R48 | anchor: A37
A driver assesses short-term illness fitness, while the Bureau participates when a long-term condition may affect driving. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R49 | anchor: A37
A license examiner can help determine when and how a person with a long-term condition can drive and whether special equipment is needed. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R50 | anchor: A37
A condition affecting alertness may still allow Maine licensing when it is shown to be stable and well controlled. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R51 | anchor: A37
Some physical disabilities require extra training or vehicle equipment and may produce a license restriction. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R52 | anchor: A37
A changed medical condition or newly used special equipment may require a driving evaluation to assess continued safe vehicle control. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R53 | anchor: A24
Sleep needs differ: the manual describes some people managing with 6 hours and others needing 10. [A24]
Source: [A24 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec03-R54 | anchor: A27
The manual recommends hands-free or speakerphone equipment for an in-vehicle phone. [A27]
Source: [A27 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-R55 | anchor: A32
Maine offers an ignition-interlock program for OUI offenders. [A32]
Source: [A32 -> pdf-0032]
